title: Corinthian Democracy
text:
In the early 1980s Brazil was still ruled by a military government, and football clubs were run in an authoritarian way too. Players were often locked up in hotels for days before matches, a practice called concentracao, and had little say in their own lives.

In 1981 Corinthians, one of Sao Paulo's biggest clubs, was in trouble. A new club president appointed a young sociologist, Adilson Monteiro Alves, as director of football. With the team's leading players, especially the midfielder Socrates, a qualified doctor, the left back Wladimir and the young striker Casagrande, he began to share decisions. Everyone at the club, from the star players to the kit men, had one vote on questions such as training times, travel, signings and whether players should be confined before games. Concentracao was dropped for married players and became optional.

The team played freely and won. Corinthians took the Sao Paulo state championship in 1982 and 1983. Players wore shirts with the words Democracia Corinthiana, and before Brazil's 1982 elections they urged fans to vote. For the 1983 final the team walked out behind a banner reading "Win or lose, but always with democracy."

The experiment faded after 1984. Socrates had promised to stay in Brazil if Congress approved direct presidential elections; when the amendment failed, he left for Italy. But the movement became a symbol of Brazil's return to democracy, which came in 1985.
lesson: A team that decides together can be both freer and more successful. Giving people a real voice in their work often raises their commitment to it.
people: Socrates, Wladimir, Walter Casagrande, Adilson Monteiro Alves
source: Brazilian press reports; Socrates and Ricardo Gozzi, Democracia Corintiana: a utopia em jogo (2002)
